steps.title: An action becomes a job, a job becomes tasks
steps.plain: count() is an action, so Spark starts a job, split into stages, split into tasks: one task per partition, run by the 2 cores of this machine. Surprise: 8 Parquet files became only 2 read tasks. Spark packs small files together (up to spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, 128 MB) and aims for about one split per core, so 8 small files are read by 2 tasks. Then a tiny final stage adds up the partial counts. Result: 2,000,000 rows in 222 ms.
logs: setup: 2,000,000 orders in 8 Parquet files; 5,000 customers in 1 file

steps.title: More partitions, more tasks, more waves
steps.plain: repartition(40) asks for 40 partitions. The job now has a shuffle (a stage that writes 8 pieces, a stage that reads 40), and the second stage has 40 tasks running two at a time: about 20 waves. More partitions than cores only helps when each task has real work; here it added overhead (546 ms).

steps.title: Transformations run nothing
steps.plain: filter, withColumn and select only describe what you want. Spark builds a plan and returns immediately: zero jobs, zero tasks, no data read. This is lazy evaluation.

steps.title: The action runs the whole plan
steps.plain: collect() is an action. Now Spark optimises the plan, reads only the columns it needs, and runs. Because we asked for 5 rows, it stops early: the first task found 5 rows and the job ended (134 ms).

steps.title: Narrow: each task works alone
steps.plain: filter and select are narrow: each output partition comes from one input partition, so every task works on its own file with no data moving between them. One stage (plus a tiny final count). 199,615 rows matched in 245 ms.

steps.title: Wide: groupBy needs a shuffle
steps.plain: groupBy(customer_id) is wide: all orders of one customer must end up in the same task, wherever they started. Stage 1 reads, pre-aggregates and writes shuffle files by customer_id; stage 2 reads its share of every file and finishes the sum. Look at shuffle write and read in the stages panel, and the Exchange in the plan. 527 ms.

steps.title: Four plans for one query
steps.plain: Spark turns your code into four plans. Parsed: what you wrote. Analysed: names and types resolved. Optimised (Catalyst): rules rewrite it, e.g. 'amount * 2 / 2' is simplified, filters are pushed below the join and down into the Parquet scan, and only the needed columns are read. Physical: how it will actually run (scans, exchanges, join strategy).

steps.plain: Look at the physical plan's FileScan nodes: PushedFilters lists the filters handed to the Parquet reader, and ReadSchema lists only the columns needed. Parquet files keep min and max per row group, so whole chunks are skipped without being read. Ran in 439 ms.

steps.title: One hot key: one slow task
steps.plain: 40% of these orders belong to customer 0 (think 'guest checkout'). In a sort-merge join, every row of customer 0 goes to the same task. In the join stage, one bar is much longer than the rest: everyone waits for it. 1260 ms. Recorded: the join stage has 16 tasks; the slowest took 234 ms while the median took 51 ms.

skewed.join(customers, 'customer_id').groupBy('name').agg(F.sum('amount'))

steps.title: AQE splits the hot partition
steps.plain: With adaptive query execution on, Spark looks at the real shuffle sizes after the first stage, sees one partition far bigger than the others, and splits it into several tasks, each joined with a copy of the matching rows from the other side. Recorded: the join stage went from 16 tasks to 23, and its slowest task from 234 ms to 57 ms (median 51 → 42 ms). Whole query: 1068 ms vs 1260 ms. One limit worth knowing: AQE can only split along the first stage's outputs, so a skewed partition can never be cut into more pieces than that stage had tasks. Thresholds were lowered for laptop scale (skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes 1 MB instead of 256 MB).

steps.title: With cache: the second action reads memory
steps.plain: cache() marks the result to be kept in memory. The first action still computes it (429 ms) and stores it; the next reads the stored result: 50 ms. The plan now starts from InMemoryTableScan. Cache only what you reuse, and unpersist it after: memory is shared with everything else.

base.count()   # computes and fills the cache
base.count()   # reads from memory
